Bad: This Windows version no longer receives security updates. Upgrade to Windows 11 if the hardware allows it, or plan to replace the device.
Until then: keep the browser updated, avoid installing unknown software, and keep backups current.

rules.forecast: Out-of-support systems accumulate unpatched vulnerabilities every month; the risk of malware and data theft grows steadily over time.

Normal: Windows 10 support (including consumer ESU) ends 2027-10-12. The 'Can move to Windows 11' row in this report says whether this PC can upgrade; plan the upgrade or replacement before then.
Windows' own check says this PC cannot move to Windows 11; the detail line names the reason.
If the reason is the TPM or Secure Boot, it can often be switched on in the firmware (BIOS/UEFI) settings, and Windows re-checks on its own later. An unsupported processor cannot be fixed.
Windows 10 security updates for home PCs end 2027-10-12 (with ESU); company PCs need Microsoft's paid Extended Security Updates. Plan to replace PCs that cannot upgrade.

rules.forecast: Once Windows 10 updates stop, every month adds security holes that will never be fixed on this PC.

Normal: Open Settings > Windows Update and install pending updates, then restart.
Bad: No successful update in over two months. Open Settings > Windows Update and install updates now.
If updates keep failing, run the Windows Update troubleshooter (Settings > System > Troubleshoot).

rules.forecast: Most real-world infections exploit vulnerabilities that were already patched — staying current is the single cheapest protection.

Normal: Restart the PC when convenient — updates only finish installing after a restart, and very long uptimes accumulate degraded state.
A restart is pending — updates or repairs are waiting to complete. Restart when convenient.
Install the waiting updates from Settings > Windows Update.
Bad: A large backlog of updates is waiting. Install them now — set aside time for one or two restarts.
The same update failed repeatedly — the Windows Update stack may be damaged.
Run the Windows Update troubleshooter first; if it persists, run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' then 'sfc /scannow' from an admin prompt.

Normal: The Windows Time service is not running right now (it often runs on demand). If the clock shows the wrong time, sync it: Settings > Time & language > Date & time > Sync now.
A wrong clock breaks secure websites, updates, and activation.

Bad: Windows is not activated. Open Settings > System > Activation to fix it — a linked digital license or a genuine product key.
Avoid 'activators' found online: they are a common malware delivery method.

Normal: The genuine state could not be fully validated offline — this is usually harmless; re-check after the next Windows Update.
Bad: Windows reports a non-genuine or tampered license. If you bought this PC or key legitimately, contact the seller or Microsoft support.
If a crack/'activator' was ever used on this machine, treat it as potentially compromised: run a full antivirus scan.
Windows is activated against a KMS server on this very machine — the signature of activation cracks (KMS emulators), which frequently bundle malware.
Run a full antivirus scan, then buy a legitimate license and activate normally (Settings > System > Activation).

rules.forecast: Machines with activation cracks have a far higher rate of infostealer infections — passwords and browser data are the usual target.
